---
title: "Retention indices and spectral identification"
description: "Alkane anchors, onset-based retention calibration, spectral distances, ion weighting and scalable matching."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

Deconvolution estimates a compound's elution profile and spectrum. Identification
then combines two kinds of evidence: when the compound elutes relative to an
alkane ladder, and how closely its spectrum resembles a reference. GCMSprime
first filters candidates by retention index and column class, then ranks their
spectral agreement. The [library-search tutorial](library-search.html) gives
the executable workflow.

## Identification algorithm

1. Identify informative alkane peaks from their diagnostic fragment series and
   molecular-ion evidence; retain an increasing carbon-number sequence.
2. Estimate a narrow-peak width curve and calculate comparable onset-based
   timing coordinates for standard and sample compounds.
3. Fit a smooth monotone map from these coordinates to alkane indices.
4. Restrict references to the chosen phase class and RI tolerance. Retain
   provenance for measured, predicted or explicitly assigned column classes.
5. Restrict each reference to the query's acquired mass bins and calculate the
   requested spectral distances, optional ion weights and count convention.
6. Return the best `n_matches` per method, with RI differences and spectral
   diagnostics. Add tentative annotations to the unchanged factorization.

## Alkane identification and RI calibration

The standard is identified using the alkyl-fragment series at m/z 43, 57, 71, 85, 99 and 113, together with the molecular ion at \(M=14c+2\) for an n-alkane with \(c\) carbons. The molecular-ion signal is corrected for the carbon-13 isotope contribution of the neighbouring alkyl ion. Minimum molecular-ion evidence and fragment-series abundance screen candidates; a maximum-weight increasing carbon-number sequence resolves duplicate maxima and inconsistent assignments. Supply the known carbon range when available. All candidates and their acceptance decisions are retained for inspection.

The retention coordinate follows

\[
t^\star=t_{\mathrm{onset}}+\frac{w_{\mathrm{small}}(t_{\mathrm{onset}})}2.
\]

Onset is the leading crossing at 1% of the background-corrected peak height. The local calibrated narrow-peak PSF supplies the full width at the same 1% height. Pass it through `psf=fit$psf_standard`; a time-varying PSF gives a smoothly varying local duration. If no PSF is supplied, a smooth lower envelope of the standard peak widths estimates the small-peak duration. This reduces the influence of overloaded or tailing peaks on the retention coordinate. Both standard peaks and recovered sample profiles use this timing convention. The relative-height fraction is configurable through `control=list(fraction=.01)`.

A smoothing spline maps \(t^\star_c\) to \(100c\); monotone interpolation through its fitted anchor values preserves the chromatographic ordering. Smoothing is selected by GCV unless `spar` is supplied. Predictions outside the accepted standard range remain unassigned by default. Verified anchors can be supplied directly, including a `narrow_width` column when timing fitted profiles.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
cal$anchors[, c("carbon", "apex", "start", "narrow_width",
                 "retention_time", "RI", "residual")]
cal$candidates
predict(cal, c(10, 20, 30))
```

This smooth calibration extends the alkane-index construction of [van den Dool & Kratz (1963)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0021-9673(01)80947-X). [NIST describes the standard RI conventions](https://webbook.nist.gov/chemistry/gc-ri/). Use a ladder acquired with the sample's column and chromatographic programme.

The Excel Run sheet records the width source and timing convention. `GCMSdeco()` reuses its stored standard PSF automatically when identification is requested.

## Column-specific retention constraints

`phase="DB1"`, `"DB5"` and `"DBWAX"` select nonpolar, semi-standard nonpolar and polar RI classes. Only references satisfying

\[
|I_{\mathrm{sample}}-I_{\mathrm{reference}}|\leq\texttt{ri\_tolerance}
\]

are scored. The closest RI measurement is used when a reference has several measurements on the selected phase class. Predicted RI records retain their provenance in the match table. Uncalibrated queries and spectra without eligible references remain visible in the query diagnostics.

MSP exports sometimes contain RI values without a column class. These remain unassigned to a phase. If the library's documentation establishes their column class, pass, for example, `unknown_phase="DB5"` explicitly. `ri_tolerance=Inf` requests spectral-only searching. It is useful for evaluating spectral scores separately from RI filtering.

NIST/OpenChrom comment summaries such as `SemiStdNP=1000 StdNP=990 StdPolar=1300` retain their DB5, DB1 and DBWAX column classes during import. Slash-delimited uncertainty summaries remain available in the raw RI value. For an explicitly justified benchmark assignment, `unknown_phase="DB5"` also admits unlabelled RI values. These matches carry `ri_assumed=TRUE`, and the Excel and MSP reports state the assignment. References with missing RIs remain excluded from a constrained search.

## Spectral comparisons and angular distance

For acquired-bin ion vectors \(a,b\), let \(N=\sum a_j\), \(p=a/N\) and \(q=b/\sum b_j\). References are restricted to the query's acquired mass bins, including bins with zero query intensity. Let \(w_j\geq0\) denote optional ion weights, with \(w_j=1\) by default.

Weighted cosine similarity is

\[
C_w(a,b)=\frac{\sum_j w_j a_jb_j}
 {\sqrt{\sum_jw_ja_j^2}\sqrt{\sum_jw_jb_j^2}}.
\]

`cosine` returns distance \(1-C_w^2\). `stein_scott` applies the same calculation after transforming intensities to \(I^{0.6}(m/z)^3\), following [Stein & Scott (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1016/1044-0305(94)87009-8) and [Kim et al. (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts083).

`angular` and `stein_scott_angular` instead return the corresponding angle

\[
\theta_w=\arccos C_w.
\]

With fixed positive weights, this is geodesic distance between the unit vectors obtained from \(\sqrt w\,a\) and \(\sqrt w\,b\), with the Stein–Scott transform added when requested. It satisfies the triangle inequality. Zero weights omit ions, and a nonzero weighted norm is required. Since intensities are nonnegative, \(0\leq\theta_w\leq\pi/2\). Angular distance ranks references in the same order as its cosine counterpart: the geometric metric property changes, while retrieval accuracy stays the same. The native search shares the ranking key, avoiding extra rounding ties from `acos()`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
w <- library_ion_weights(lib)
matches <- library_search(fit, lib, calibration=cal, phase="DB5",
  ri_tolerance=30, method=c("angular", "stein_scott_angular"),
  ion_weights=w, n_matches=5)
```

### Probability distances and sample counts

`hellinger` uses the weighted square-root distance

\[
H_w(p,q)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2W}\sum_jw_j(\sqrt{p_j}-\sqrt{q_j})^2},
\qquad W=\max_jw_j.
\]

For \(r=(p+q)/2\), define the weighted Jensen–Shannon divergence

\[
J_w(p,q)=\frac12\sum_jw_j\left[p_j\log\frac{p_j}{r_j}
                              +q_j\log\frac{q_j}{r_j}\right].
\]

`jensen_shannon` returns \(\sqrt{J_w/(W\log2)}\). Zero contributions use \(0\log0=0\). The common bound \(W\) puts these probability distances on a 0–1 scale.

MSP libraries generally provide relative intensities, with unknown original ion totals. The default `reference_count="auto"` uses an explicit `Pseudocount`/`Ion_total` tag when supplied; otherwise it assigns the reference the same total as the sample spectrum. `reference_count="query"` always uses this balanced convention, and `"library"` uses the stored library intensity scale.

For effective reference total \(M\), the multinomial divergence is

\[
D_w=2\sum_jw_j\left[Np_j\log\frac{p_j}{u_j}
                   +Mq_j\log\frac{q_j}{u_j}\right],
\qquad u=\frac{Np+Mq}{N+M}.
\]

With \(M=N\), it simplifies to

\[
\boxed{D_w=4N J_w(p,q).}
\]

Thus balanced multinomial deviance has the same ranking as weighted Jensen–Shannon, with its absolute scale determined by the sample's retained pseudocount. At a fixed \(N\), it is symmetric in the spectral shapes. Each ion contributes a nonnegative Jensen gap. Nonconstant weights give an importance-weighted composite divergence; uniform weights and known totals give the ordinary multinomial likelihood-ratio statistic. Native evaluation uses nonnegative scalar gaps and a local series near equality, avoiding cancellation amplified by large counts.

`query_total` preserves the sample total; `library_total` records the reference's stored/restored total. `reference_total` and `reference_count` show the effective comparison convention, and `library_mass_coverage` records acquisition coverage. For an L1-normalized matrix, supply its original totals through `pseudocount=`. A `GCMSdeco` fit supplies them automatically. Explicit count tags also preserve totals through MSP export and re-import.

Scores run from 0 to 1000, with larger values better. Angular scores are \(1000(1-2\theta/\pi)\); distances remain in radians. Probability and count-based scores follow the definitions in [library_search()](../reference/library_search.html). Compare scores within a method and weighting convention.

## Ion uniqueness weights

[library_ion_weights()](../reference/library_ion_weights.html) computes smoothed inverse-document-frequency weights. If \(L\) nonempty reference spectra are available and \(d_j\) contain ion \(j\),

\[
w_j\propto\left[1+\log\frac{L+1}{d_j+1}\right]^\alpha.
\]

Weights are normalized to mean one. An ion is counted when it reaches at least 1% of the acquired-bin base peak; `min_relative` controls this threshold. `power` sets \(\alpha\), default 1. For cosine matching, `power=2` corresponds to multiplying spectral amplitudes by the usual inverse-document-frequency factor. All search methods accept the same reusable weight vector.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
w <- library_ion_weights(lib, mass=33:550, min_relative=.01, power=1)
attr(w, "frequency")

hits <- library_search(fit, lib, calibration=cal, phase="DB5",
  method=c("multinomial", "angular"), ion_weights=w,
  reference_count="query", n_matches=5)
```

Frequency estimation reads SQLite records in bounded batches and uses native OpenMP counts. Compute the vector once per reference catalogue and reuse it for every sample. Named custom vectors are also accepted; unspecified masses retain weight one. Frequency-dependent weighting has also been studied for [MS/MS library annotation](https://doi.org/10.1021/jasms.3c00353), including enhancement of frequently observed ions. The inverse-frequency option here emphasizes ion rarity, and its benefit is checked directly on EI spectra.

## Accuracy and speed

The comparison used 500 MoNA query spectra from distinct InChIKey/CAS groups, divided into 250 development and 250 validation queries. Query records and near-duplicate same-identity reference shapes (normalized L1 difference at most 0.05) were excluded, leaving 19,082 nonempty reference spectra. Ion frequencies were estimated from those references. RI filtering was disabled to measure spectral discrimination directly.

The independent validation results below give **correct first match / correct within top five**, in percent. IDF uses `power=1`; IDF² uses `power=2`, both with a 1% presence threshold.

| Method | Uniform weights | IDF | IDF² |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Stein–Scott / Stein–Scott angular | 49.6 / 60.8 | 50.0 / 61.2 | 50.0 / 60.8 |
| Cosine / angular | 36.8 / 56.0 | 37.6 / 56.4 | 37.6 / 56.0 |
| Hellinger | 46.4 / 68.8 | 46.8 / 67.2 | 48.8 / 66.0 |
| Jensen–Shannon / balanced multinomial | 45.6 / 67.6 | 46.8 / 67.6 | 47.6 / 65.6 |

Using arbitrary stored library intensity totals for multinomial deviance gives 9.2% first-match and 19.2% top-five recovery in this comparison. Balancing unknown totals to the sample avoids that scale dependence. Rarity weighting gives modest first-match gains, with some top-five trade-offs; uniform weights remain the default. Angular metrics preserve their corresponding cosine rankings exactly.

For 500 queries against the 19,082 references, using IDF weights and eight physical cores:

| Method | Search time |
|:--|--:|
| Stein–Scott | 0.52 s |
| Cosine | 0.45 s |
| Angular | 0.44 s |
| Stein–Scott angular | 0.58 s |
| Hellinger | 0.57 s |
| Jensen–Shannon | 2.14 s |
| Balanced multinomial | 2.15 s |

Preparing the reusable IDF weights took 0.35 s. Timings include preparing and searching the imported library, on an HP ZBook Fury G8 with an Intel i9-11950H and eight physical cores. The [benchmark script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/blob/master/benchmarks/library_search_weights.R) and [aggregate results](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime/tree/master/benchmarks/results) are available in the repository.

## Retention-index conventions and interpretation

For temperature-programmed GC, the conventional adjacent-alkane index is
linear in retention time. Isothermal Kováts indices use adjusted log retention
times. These conventions and column metadata are summarized by
[NIST](https://webbook.nist.gov/chemistry/gc-ri/). GCMSprime's smooth calibration
uses its onset-based coordinate consistently for standards and resolved sample
profiles, with alkane targets `100 * carbon`.

A spectral score expresses agreement under its stated transformation and
weighting. The reported best matches are tentative compound annotations;
reference standards, diagnostic chemistry and the chromatographic programme
provide additional identification evidence. In multisample fits, consensus IDs
link occurrences; each occurrence can use its own standard-derived RI.
